claims.text: The compared Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy and its quaternary and ternary subsets have equiatomic compositions.
All compared alloys have single-phase FCC microstructures after thermomechanical processing.
All compared alloys are prepared using identical thermomechanical processing.
Constituent count alone is inadequate to determine alloy behavior, whereas the chemical identities and interactions of the elements matter.
Removing one or more constituents systematically changes local chemical short-range order.
Changes in local chemical short-range order alter the spatial distribution of stacking-fault energies.
Differences in the stacking-fault-energy landscape alter dislocation nucleation, mobility, and twinning.
Mn in the equiatomic quinary alloy promotes a spatially variable stacking-fault energy through local chemical interactions.
Mn-enhanced local interactions increase partial-dislocation nucleation and the formation of extensive stacking-fault networks.
Quaternary and ternary subsets lacking one or more constituents have a more uniform or otherwise different stacking-fault-energy distribution than the quinary alloy.
Composition-dependent defect dynamics account for differences in strain hardening, ductility, and failure mode.
Partial-dislocation activity can produce stable three-dimensional stacking-fault networks that contribute to strain hardening.
Relative to the quinary baseline, quaternary and especially ternary alloys will exhibit fewer or less spatially distributed stacking faults and nanotwins.
Relative to the quinary baseline, quaternary and especially ternary alloys will have lower strain-hardening rates.
Relative to the quinary baseline, quaternary and especially ternary alloys will likely have reduced ductility.
The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni baseline has established stacking-fault-network formation and dislocation dynamics.
Holding strain rate, temperature, stress state, processing, and environment fixed makes composition the source of observed differences.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to non-equiatomic compositions, different thermal histories, or mechanical tests outside the specified conditions.
